## Study III: Clinical Dynamics (Simultaneous iEEG/EEG)

### Spatial and Temporal Correlation Analysis

Source localization was inconclusive for connectivity-informed methods in Study II — comparable to, but not clearly better than, standard methods (Section 3.2.1). Because these methods are designed to capture distributed activity rather than a single focal source, we instead tested whether they better reproduce the overall pattern of activity, as the simulation results in Section 3.1 suggest they should.

Of the four subjects with usable simultaneous EEG/iEEG data (Section 2.1.3), two show a visible interictal spike on the scalp EEG; the remaining two have deep sources producing no visible spike on the EEG despite clear intracranial evidence of the same interictal discharge, and are reported in the supplementary material rather than the main text below (<!-- supp figure (sub-12/sub-50: wCSET - competitor paired differences, per channel/timepoint) -->). For each subject we compared wCSET against every competitor at the level of individual channels (temporal correlation: how well each channel's own time-course matches the true intracranial recording) and individual timepoints (spatial correlation: how well the pattern across channels matches at each instant), using a paired t-test with an autocorrelation-corrected effective sample size (n_eff) in place of the raw channel/timepoint count, since neighbouring channels and timepoints from the same subject and spike are not independent observations.

```{python filename="results_intra_vieeg_significance.py"}
#| output: false
import mindmap as mm

# reuses METHODS/COLORS already defined above in plot_configuration.py, so
# method colors stay consistent with every other figure in this document.
# beltrami (6th competitor, clinical-only, see plot_configuration.py's note)
# is added to COMPETITORS below in processing_intra.qmd's own method order
# (["wcset", "sloreta", "cset", "dspm", "wmne", "beltrami"]) rather than
# appended after METHODS's order, so this cell's stat.ttest_ess() calls stay
# an exact, byte-identical match to the ones already cached by that file's
# Statistics section.

# combined suite (every sub-*/ subfolder concatenated) built and stats-cached
# by processing_intra.qmd's Statistics section - loaded here directly, never
# combined via concat() in this document.
vieeg_metrics = mm.metric.MetricSuite.load("./results/intra/combined")

# Only 4 subjects total (fixed), and 2 of them (12, 50) have deep sources with
# no visible spike on scalp EEG -- their EEG-derived source reconstruction
# (and therefore virtual iEEG) starts from an inherently less reliable signal
# than 34/48's. Stats are still computed for all 4 (SUBJECT_ORDER) - reused
# by the supplementary material - but the main-text figure below only plots
# MAIN_SUBJECTS (34/48); 12/50 are reported in the supplementary material
# instead (see prose above).
SUBJECT_ORDER = ["34", "48", "12", "50"]
MAIN_SUBJECTS = ["48", "34"]
SUBJECT_TITLES = {
    "34": "Subject 2",
    "48": "Subject 1",
    "12": "sub-12\n(no visible EEG spike)",
    "50": "sub-50\n(no visible EEG spike)",
}

# Only 4 subjects - too few for subject-level pairing (pairing_col="Subject"
# would treat n=4 as the sample size, no real power). Channels/timepoints
# within one subject are numerous but NOT independent (spatially/temporally
# correlated), so a plain Wilcoxon/t-test paired across them would overstate
# significance. Fix: an autocorrelation-corrected effective sample size
# (Thiebaux & Zwiers, 1984) in place of the raw channel/timepoint count -
# mindmap.core.stats.effective_sample_size, via
# suite.stat.ttest_ess(...) - see
# mindmap/tutorials/analysis/metrics/metricsuite-intra-vieeg.ipynb, which
# this cell adapts directly (measured lag-1 autocorrelation of the
# wCSET-competitor difference series on this exact data: 0.45-0.83 for
# timepoints, 0.16-0.52 for channels - large enough that the correction has
# real bite, not just a formality).
COMPETITORS = ["sloreta", "cset", "dspm", "wmne", "beltrami"]


def paired_diffs(subject, metric, coord):
    # exact post-dropna order already computed and cached by
    # processing_intra.qmd's Statistics section - reused verbatim both to
    # rebuild this diffs array and to keep the stat.ttest_ess() call
    # below (part of the cache key) an instant cache hit rather than a
    # silent recompute under a different order.
    order = vieeg_metrics.metadata["derived"]["subject_order"][subject][metric]
    df_sub = vieeg_metrics.to_df(metrics=metric, filters={"Subject": subject})
    wide = df_sub.pivot_table(index=coord, columns="Method", values="Value", aggfunc="mean").reindex(order)
    wide = wide.dropna(subset=["wcset"] + COMPETITORS)
    return {c: (wide["wcset"] - wide[c]).to_numpy() for c in COMPETITORS}, wide.index.tolist()


METRIC_BLOCKS = [
    ("correlation_temporal", "channel", "Temporal corr.\n(diff per channel)"),
    ("correlation_spatial", "times", "Spatial corr.\n(diff per timepoint)"),
]

# statistics quoted in the prose below and drawn by the figure at the end of
# this section are collected into these two dicts, keyed by (subject,
# metric) - so the figure and the prose numbers come from exactly the same
# stat.ttest_ess() call, run once here.
vieeg_results = {}
vieeg_diffs = {}

for metric, coord, ylabel in METRIC_BLOCKS:
    for subject in SUBJECT_ORDER:
        diffs, order = paired_diffs(subject, metric, coord)
        # identical call to the one already cached by processing_intra.qmd's
        # Statistics section.
        vieeg_results[(subject, metric)] = vieeg_metrics.stat.ttest_ess(
            metric, group_by="Method", comparisons=vieeg_metrics.stat.build_comparisons(["wcset"], COMPETITORS),
            pairing_col=coord, subject_order=order, filters={"Subject": subject},
        )
        vieeg_diffs[(subject, metric)] = diffs

# statistics quoted in the prose below.
def _p(subject, metric, competitor):
    return competitor_row(vieeg_results[(subject, metric)], competitor)["p_corrected"]

def _neff(subject, metric, competitor):
    return competitor_row(vieeg_results[(subject, metric)], competitor)["n_eff"]

def _winrate(subject, metric, competitor):
    return vieeg_metrics.metadata["derived"]["win_rate"][f"{subject}|{metric}|{competitor}"]

def _dz(subject, metric, competitor):
    # ttest_ess's own effect size (Cohen's dz on the wcset-competitor
    # difference series) - positive means wCSET wins, matching the
    # win-rate/diff sign convention used elsewhere in this cell.
    return competitor_row(vieeg_results[(subject, metric)], competitor)["effect_size"]

vieeg_48_spatial_p_cset = fmt_p(_p("48", "correlation_spatial", "cset"))
vieeg_48_spatial_p_sloreta = fmt_p(_p("48", "correlation_spatial", "sloreta"))
vieeg_48_spatial_p_dspm = fmt_p(_p("48", "correlation_spatial", "dspm"))
vieeg_48_spatial_p_wmne = fmt_p(_p("48", "correlation_spatial", "wmne"))
vieeg_48_spatial_p_beltrami = fmt_p(_p("48", "correlation_spatial", "beltrami"))
vieeg_48_spatial_neff_cset = f"{_neff('48', 'correlation_spatial', 'cset'):.0f}"
vieeg_48_spatial_neff_sloreta = f"{_neff('48', 'correlation_spatial', 'sloreta'):.0f}"
vieeg_48_spatial_neff_dspm = f"{_neff('48', 'correlation_spatial', 'dspm'):.0f}"
vieeg_48_spatial_neff_wmne = f"{_neff('48', 'correlation_spatial', 'wmne'):.0f}"
vieeg_48_spatial_neff_beltrami = f"{_neff('48', 'correlation_spatial', 'beltrami'):.0f}"
vieeg_48_spatial_dz_cset = fmt_stat(_dz("48", "correlation_spatial", "cset"))
vieeg_48_spatial_dz_sloreta = fmt_stat(_dz("48", "correlation_spatial", "sloreta"))
vieeg_48_spatial_dz_dspm = fmt_stat(_dz("48", "correlation_spatial", "dspm"))
vieeg_48_spatial_dz_wmne = fmt_stat(_dz("48", "correlation_spatial", "wmne"))
vieeg_48_spatial_dz_beltrami = fmt_stat(_dz("48", "correlation_spatial", "beltrami"))

# excludes beltrami deliberately: its raw per-timepoint win-rate sits below
# chance (unlike the other four) even though the autocorrelation-corrected
# paired test below still finds it significantly worse than wCSET on
# average - folding it into this range would make the "above chance"
# framing wrong. Reported separately in the prose instead.
_sub48_spatial_winrates = [_winrate("48", "correlation_spatial", c) for c in ["cset", "sloreta", "dspm", "wmne"]]
vieeg_48_winrate_min = f"{min(_sub48_spatial_winrates) * 100:.0f}"
vieeg_48_winrate_max = f"{max(_sub48_spatial_winrates) * 100:.0f}"
vieeg_48_winrate_pp_min = f"{(min(_sub48_spatial_winrates) - 0.5) * 100:.0f}"
vieeg_48_winrate_pp_max = f"{(max(_sub48_spatial_winrates) - 0.5) * 100:.0f}"
vieeg_48_beltrami_winrate = f"{_winrate('48', 'correlation_spatial', 'beltrami') * 100:.0f}"

vieeg_48_temporal_p_wmne = fmt_p(_p("48", "correlation_temporal", "wmne"))
vieeg_48_temporal_dz_wmne = fmt_stat(_dz("48", "correlation_temporal", "wmne"))
vieeg_48_temporal_p_beltrami = fmt_p(_p("48", "correlation_temporal", "beltrami"))
vieeg_48_temporal_dz_beltrami = fmt_stat(_dz("48", "correlation_temporal", "beltrami"))

vieeg_34_temporal_p_cset = fmt_p(_p("34", "correlation_temporal", "cset"))
vieeg_34_temporal_neff_cset = f"{_neff('34', 'correlation_temporal', 'cset'):.0f}"
vieeg_34_temporal_winrate_cset = f"{_winrate('34', 'correlation_temporal', 'cset') * 100:.0f}"
vieeg_34_temporal_dz_cset = fmt_stat(_dz("34", "correlation_temporal", "cset"))
vieeg_34_temporal_p_beltrami = fmt_p(_p("34", "correlation_temporal", "beltrami"))
vieeg_34_temporal_neff_beltrami = f"{_neff('34', 'correlation_temporal', 'beltrami'):.0f}"
vieeg_34_temporal_winrate_beltrami = f"{_winrate('34', 'correlation_temporal', 'beltrami') * 100:.0f}"
vieeg_34_temporal_dz_beltrami = fmt_stat(_dz("34", "correlation_temporal", "beltrami"))
vieeg_34_spatial_p_cset = fmt_p(_p("34", "correlation_spatial", "cset"))
vieeg_34_spatial_dz_cset = fmt_stat(_dz("34", "correlation_spatial", "cset"))
vieeg_34_spatial_p_beltrami = fmt_p(_p("34", "correlation_spatial", "beltrami"))
vieeg_34_spatial_dz_beltrami = fmt_stat(_dz("34", "correlation_spatial", "beltrami"))
```

Among the subjects with a visible EEG spike, the two responded very differently. Subject 1 showed the clearest advantage for wCSET: spatial correlation was significantly higher than sLORETA, dSPM, wMNE, and CSET (vs. CSET p_corrected `{python} vieeg_48_spatial_p_cset`, dz=`{python} vieeg_48_spatial_dz_cset`, n_eff=`{python} vieeg_48_spatial_neff_cset`; vs. sLORETA p_corrected `{python} vieeg_48_spatial_p_sloreta`, dz=`{python} vieeg_48_spatial_dz_sloreta`, n_eff=`{python} vieeg_48_spatial_neff_sloreta`; vs. dSPM p_corrected `{python} vieeg_48_spatial_p_dspm`, dz=`{python} vieeg_48_spatial_dz_dspm`, n_eff=`{python} vieeg_48_spatial_neff_dspm`; vs. wMNE p_corrected `{python} vieeg_48_spatial_p_wmne`, dz=`{python} vieeg_48_spatial_dz_wmne`, n_eff=`{python} vieeg_48_spatial_neff_wmne`), with wCSET winning `{python} vieeg_48_winrate_min`–`{python} vieeg_48_winrate_max`% of timepoints against these four competitors (`{python} vieeg_48_winrate_pp_min`–`{python} vieeg_48_winrate_pp_max` percentage points above chance). Temporal correlation was more modest: only the comparison against wMNE remained significant after correction (p_corrected `{python} vieeg_48_temporal_p_wmne`, dz=`{python} vieeg_48_temporal_dz_wmne`); sLORETA, dSPM, and CSET did not differ significantly. Against Beltrami, the pattern reversed: spatial correlation was significantly *lower* for wCSET (p_corrected `{python} vieeg_48_spatial_p_beltrami`, dz=`{python} vieeg_48_spatial_dz_beltrami`, n_eff=`{python} vieeg_48_spatial_neff_beltrami`) — a smaller effect than the differences against the other four competitors — and wCSET won only `{python} vieeg_48_beltrami_winrate`% of individual timepoints, below the 50% chance level; temporal correlation against Beltrami did not differ significantly (p_corrected `{python} vieeg_48_temporal_p_beltrami`, dz=`{python} vieeg_48_temporal_dz_beltrami`).

Subject 2 did not reproduce this pattern: the only significant differences across either metric were a temporal advantage over CSET (p_corrected `{python} vieeg_34_temporal_p_cset`, dz=`{python} vieeg_34_temporal_dz_cset`, n_eff=`{python} vieeg_34_temporal_neff_cset`, wCSET winning `{python} vieeg_34_temporal_winrate_cset`% of channels) and a temporal *disadvantage* against Beltrami (p_corrected `{python} vieeg_34_temporal_p_beltrami`, dz=`{python} vieeg_34_temporal_dz_beltrami`, n_eff=`{python} vieeg_34_temporal_neff_beltrami`, wCSET winning only `{python} vieeg_34_temporal_winrate_beltrami`% of channels) — wCSET did not differ significantly from any other competitor in either metric (spatial: CSET p_corrected `{python} vieeg_34_spatial_p_cset`, dz=`{python} vieeg_34_spatial_dz_cset`; Beltrami p_corrected `{python} vieeg_34_spatial_p_beltrami`, dz=`{python} vieeg_34_spatial_dz_beltrami`).


```{python filename="results_intra_vieeg_significance_plot.py"}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Per-channel temporal-correlation differences (top row) and per-timepoint spatial-correlation differences (bottom row), wCSET minus each competitor, for the two subjects with a visible scalp EEG spike (sub-12/sub-50 are reported in the supplementary material). Win rate relative to the 50% chance line and effective sample size (n_eff) are annotated above each box. Stars mark significance from an autocorrelation-corrected paired t-test (ttest_ess)."
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt


def draw_diff_panel(ax, subject, metric, coord, title=None):
    diffs = vieeg_diffs[(subject, metric)]
    results = vieeg_results[(subject, metric)]

    data = [diffs[c] for c in COMPETITORS]
    bp = ax.boxplot(data, positions=range(len(COMPETITORS)), widths=0.5,
                     patch_artist=True, showfliers=False, zorder=2)
    for patch, c in zip(bp["boxes"], COMPETITORS):
        patch.set_facecolor(COLORS[c])
        patch.set_alpha(0.55)
    for element in ["whiskers", "caps", "medians"]:
        for line in bp[element]:
            line.set_color("#333333")

    rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
    for i, c in enumerate(COMPETITORS):
        y = diffs[c]
        x = i + rng.uniform(-0.15, 0.15, size=len(y))
        point_colors = np.where(y > 0, "tab:green", "tab:red")
        ax.scatter(x, y, s=6, alpha=0.45, c=point_colors, linewidths=0, zorder=3)

    ax.axhline(0, color="black", linewidth=1, linestyle="--", zorder=1)
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(COMPETITORS)))
    ax.set_xticklabels(COMPETITORS, fontsize=8)

    ymax, ymin = max(np.max(d) for d in data), min(np.min(d) for d in data)
    span = ymax - ymin
    for i, c in enumerate(COMPETITORS):
        row = competitor_row(results, c)
        # relative to the 50% chance line, not the raw win-rate - +17%/-13%
        # reads instantly (sign+color = direction, magnitude = how far from
        # a coin flip), where "37% vs. 67%" both need mentally subtracting
        # 50% first to compare. Read from processing_intra.qmd's precomputed
        # metadata["derived"], not recomputed here (a genuine derived stat).
        rel_win = vieeg_metrics.metadata["derived"]["win_rate"][f"{subject}|{metric}|{c}"] - 0.5
        p = row["p_corrected"]
        stars = "***" if p < 0.001 else "**" if p < 0.01 else "*" if p < 0.05 else "ns"
        win_color = "tab:green" if rel_win > 0 else "tab:red"
        ax.text(i, ymax + 0.10 * span, stars, ha="center", va="bottom", fontsize=7, color="#222222")
        ax.text(i, ymax + 0.055 * span, f"{rel_win:+.0%}", ha="center", va="bottom",
                fontsize=7.5, color=win_color, fontweight="bold")
        ax.text(i, ymax + 0.01 * span, f"n_eff={row['n_eff']:.0f}", ha="center", va="bottom",
                fontsize=6, color="#666666")

    ax.set_ylim(ymin - 0.08 * span, ymax + 0.32 * span)
    if title:
        ax.set_title(title, fontsize=9)


# MAIN_SUBJECTS only (34/48) - sub-12/sub-50 (no visible EEG spike) are
# reported in the supplementary material instead (see prose above).
vieeg_fig, vieeg_axes = plt.subplots(
    len(METRIC_BLOCKS), len(MAIN_SUBJECTS),
    figsize=(4.2 * len(MAIN_SUBJECTS), 3.6 * len(METRIC_BLOCKS)),
)

for row_i, (metric, coord, ylabel) in enumerate(METRIC_BLOCKS):
    for col_i, subject in enumerate(MAIN_SUBJECTS):
        ax = vieeg_axes[row_i, col_i]
        draw_diff_panel(ax, subject, metric, coord, title=SUBJECT_TITLES[subject] if row_i == 0 else None)
        if col_i == 0:
            ax.set_ylabel(ylabel, fontsize=8)

plt.tight_layout()
```


# Discussion

## Simulation take home message

The simulation begins as a focal source and spreads across the brain, its amplitude decaying with the number of graph hops from the origin. This lets the signal propagate along neighboring dipoles but also take shortcuts via long-range tracts, allowing distant regions to rise above the noise floor that pure nearest-neighbor spread could never reach on its own — a mechanism absent from neural field models. The most physiologically detailed way to enforce this would be a neural mass model [@jansen_electroencephalogram_1995], but such models become unstable at very high mass counts, since network size and coupling strength jointly determine whether the system remains within a stable dynamical regime [@sanz-leon_mathematical_2015]. Other source-reconstruction studies therefore reduce the number of masses to around 1,000, with dipoles spaced roughly 1 cm apart [@siu_structural_2026]. At that spacing, the assumption that each dipole's effective area is much smaller than its distance to the sensors — the basis of the equivalent-dipole model that the forward solution itself depends on — begins to break down [@nunez_multi-scale_2019]. To preserve the dipole model (using ~7,600 dipoles spaced approximately 3.3 mm apart) while keeping the simulation simple enough to generate realistic EEG spikes, we adopted this patch-seeded, connectome-driven propagation model: the source itself is a spatial patch, but the propagated pattern is not necessarily one, since it can reach non-adjacent regions directly via long-range tracts rather than only spreading outward through neighbors. We do not claim that this simulation represents reality more faithfully than neural mass or neural field models, but we believe it offers insight into source-reconstruction behavior that a simple patch simulation cannot provide, while remaining tractable at high dipole counts.

A further consequence of this design is that the EEG signal's peak systematically lags the true onset of the underlying source: although the source's own amplitude is highest at the origin at onset and decays from there as it spreads, the *scalp* signal sums contributions across all active dipoles at once, so it keeps rising as the pattern reaches more of the cortex even as the origin itself fades — it is this cumulative, cross-source summation, that pushes the scalp peak to arrive only once the source has already spread considerably — consistent with the broader clinical literature on interictal discharge propagation [@vorderwulbecke_high-density_2020; @carboni_linear_2022]. This is precisely why the field favors an earlier point in the rising phase over the peak for source localization: at that point the signal is already detectable, but activity remains largely concentrated near the true onset, with only limited spread having occurred.

### Localization versus spread

Most simulation-based source-reconstruction studies focus on localization and report both location and spatial extent. At the quarter rising phase, the source is still relatively focal and largely independent from the rest of the cortex. Methods such as sLORETA and dSPM were designed to optimize localization accuracy but do not explicitly address extent; more recent methods instead prioritize extent and typically report improved results over these classical baselines. In this study, wCSET's localization error at the quarter rising phase differed significantly from every other method (Wilcoxon signed-rank vs. wCSET, paired by region, FDR-corrected; Section 3.1.1), but the direction and magnitude of that difference varied considerably. Against CSET and dSPM, wCSET was in fact modestly *less* accurate, with effect sizes small enough that, practically, these three methods localize the source about equally well at this early, focal phase. Its advantage over sLORETA was more substantial, and its advantage over wMNE was large — wMNE was the clear outlier among the five methods at this phase, not merely the weakest by a small margin. With 100 simulated regions and multiple repetitions behind each test, even small differences readily reach significance, so it is the effect sizes, not the p-values alone, that separate a meaningful gap (wMNE, and to a lesser extent sLORETA) from an essentially negligible one (CSET, dSPM). We do not report extent using the precision/recall-style metrics common in the literature [@bradley_evaluation_2016], since thresholding the reconstructed activity into a binary "active" mask would require an arbitrary and difficult-to-justify cutoff. Instead we measure spatial correlation with the ground truth, and the higher correlation already visible for wCSET and CSET at the quarter rising phase hints at a genuine improvement in extent, consistent with reports from similar connectivity- and geometry-informed methods [@wang_geometry_2026; @siu_structural_2026]. This improvement can be explained by the fact that connectivity matrices include local, neighboring connections that help define spatially coherent patches of activity.

That said, connectivity-informed source reconstruction offers more than an improvement in source extent: because it is constrained by the brain's actual connections, it also addresses the spread problem directly. We show that spatial correlation improves markedly as the signal spreads toward the EEG peak, indicating that these methods can potentially reconstruct the brain's dynamics well beyond the initial stimulus — or, in the clinical case, beyond the onset of an interictal epileptiform discharge. Irrespective of method, correlation increases toward the peak phase; part of this is simply the higher signal-to-noise ratio at that point, which is also why sLORETA's correlation rises over the same window. The much larger gain observed for wCSET and CSET, however, is better explained by the connectome-spectrum literature: as activity spreads across the cortex, its representation becomes increasingly compact in the connectome-harmonic domain, with this compactness itself tracking the signal's power [@rue-queralt_connectome_2021]. In other words, as the source spreads, it becomes progressively better described by a small number of graph harmonics — exactly the representation wCSET and CSET are built around — which explains their disproportionate gain in correlation as the peak phase approaches. What matters for comparing methods, then, is not that correlation rises for everyone as SNR improves, but the widening gap between connectivity-informed and connectivity-agnostic methods over that same window.

### Robustness to inaccuracies

To test whether any method is more robust to noise than the others, we repeated source reconstruction across a range of single-trial SNRs and connectome degradation levels, rather than the single SNR=5 level used above (Section 3.1.2). Localization error increased for every method as SNR decreased, but wMNE alone accounts for most of this pattern: already several times wCSET's error at the highest SNR tested, it degraded steadily further and remained significantly worse than wCSET across the entire SNR range tested. The other four methods — wCSET, CSET, sLORETA, and dSPM — instead behaved similarly to one another on localization error, staying low until roughly SNR=4–5 before climbing together: sLORETA's and dSPM's brief high-SNR plateaus did reach significance against wCSET, but with modest effect sizes that did not extend to lower SNR, and CSET never differed significantly from wCSET anywhere in the range tested. Spatial correlation told a cleaner story: wCSET significantly outperformed all four competitors at both the quarter rising phase and the peak across nearly the entire SNR range tested, holding even at low SNR, with effect sizes ranging from moderate to very large.

One limitation of this analysis is that SNR was calibrated on the single trial, before averaging 20 epochs into the evoked response used for reconstruction; since averaging itself raises the effective SNR of the signal that is actually reconstructed, the single-trial value we vary does not equal the SNR of the reconstructed evoked response. We did not additionally vary the number of averaged epochs, so how the two factors trade off against one another remains untested.

Degrading the connectome produced a single, monotonic decline in performance for both methods. Under permutation, CSET's spatial correlation stayed comparatively flat through 60% degradation (Section 3.1.3), which first suggested that the harmonics driving reconstruction accuracy might simply be the most robust ones, irrespective of graph frequency. We initially attempted to encode this directly, weighting harmonics with a U-shaped profile based on @sipes_integrative_2024's finding that harmonic robustness to connectome perturbation follows the gap-spectrum (the difference between consecutive eigenvalues), favoring so-called integrative harmonics (the low-frequency end of the spectrum) and segregative harmonics (the high-frequency end) over the intermediate, degenerate ones. In practice, however, retaining the high-frequency end of this U introduced visible reconstruction artifacts, likely a consequence of how sparse high-frequency harmonics are. We therefore narrowed our focus to the low-frequency harmonics alone, aligning with the broader literature, and adopted an exponential decay that weights only the low-frequency end of the spectrum — the choice that became wCSET — which improved on CSET's spatial correlation with the ground truth. Benchmarked directly against the connectome-agnostic sLORETA baseline, CSET's correlation advantage reversed into a significant deficit from 80% permutation onward, while wCSET's held significant through 80% and only became statistically indistinguishable from sLORETA at full permutation (region-paired cluster-permutation vs. sLORETA; Section 3.1.3). Localization error followed essentially the same pattern: CSET's own early advantage over sLORETA (significant through 60% permutation) likewise reversed into a significant deficit from 80% permutation onward, while wCSET's advantage — significant through 70% — never reversed into a significant deficit at any degradation level tested, including full permutation. On both metrics, the absolute gap between wCSET and CSET narrowed steadily as degradation increased, and both converged toward the connectome-agnostic sLORETA/dSPM baselines by full permutation — consistent with a fully permuted connectome carrying essentially no genuine structural information at that point, leaving both methods in much the same position as sLORETA and dSPM, which never used the connectome at all. This robustness suggests that our methods tolerate substantial rewiring while still benefiting from whatever structure remains, encouraging given the well-documented limitations of tractography, which produces substantially more false-positive than true-positive white matter bundles [@maier-hein_challenge_2017] — and it further suggests that even fairly crude connectome surrogates should support reasonable reconstruction accuracy, a hypothesis we test directly next.

### Using surrogates
We tested several ways to build a connectome surrogate for settings where subject-specific dMRI is unavailable: extrapolating a dipole-level connectome from a published atlas, relying purely on cortical geometry via our own local-connectivity rule, and the increasingly popular Laplace-Beltrami operator. We also tested whether the edge weights themselves matter, by comparing each weighted surrogate against its binarized (presence/absence) counterpart. Somewhat surprisingly, for localization error wCSET was significantly *more* accurate using every surrogate than using the true connectome itself (Section 3.1.4), though the effect sizes were only small to moderate — with 100 simulated regions behind each comparison, such consistent but modest gains are statistically robust without being dramatic in practice, and no surrogate stood out as meaningfully better than the rest. For spatial correlation, every surrogate again produced a significant increase relative to the true connectome, this time at both the quarter rising phase and the peak. Effect sizes were generally small at the quarter rising phase but grew substantially by the peak, most markedly for Beltrami — yet even so, wCSET's correlation using Beltrami, like every other surrogate, remained roughly 3–4× higher than dSPM's or sLORETA's own correlation using the *true* connectome. The binarized and weighted versions of the atlas and local surrogates performed very similarly to one another, suggesting that the precise edge weights contribute comparatively little beyond the surrogate's topology. None of the five stood out as a clear overall winner among themselves — the effect-size differences between surrogates were themselves small — even though, by this measure, all five outperformed the true connectome.

Why might dMRI-free surrogates match, or even slightly exceed, the true connectome's own reconstruction accuracy? Part of the answer is structural: wCSET's exponential weighting emphasizes only a small number of low-frequency graph harmonics, which correspond to coarse, large-scale structure — such as the hemispheric and lobar organization of the cortex — that is broadly shared across very different connectome constructions (tractography-derived, atlas-derived, or purely geometric), even when their fine-grained, high-frequency detail differs substantially. This alone would explain why the surrogates can match the true connectome, and why the exact edge weights matter so little beyond topology. It does not, on its own, explain why several surrogates slightly *exceed* it, which we think more likely reflects two further, complementary factors. First, our propagation model layers hop-based delays on top of connectome topology, so it is the distance/hop structure, not merely which regions are connected, that shapes the resulting spatiotemporal pattern; geometric surrogates such as Beltrami encode smooth spatial distance directly, which may align better with the delay structure the propagation model is actually sensitive to than the true connectome's tract-based shortcuts do, even though that same true connectome generated the data. Second, the true, subject-specific connectome is tractography-derived and therefore noisy [@maier-hein_challenge_2017]; since wCSET only ever retains a handful of low-frequency harmonics, any idiosyncratic noise in the true connectome's fine structure that leaks into those harmonics can only be a liability, never a benefit, because the reconstruction cannot use the high-frequency detail regardless. A smoother geometric surrogate has no such noise to leak, so its low-frequency harmonics may sit closer to whatever generic coarse structure the propagation model actually depends on — a regularization-like effect, akin to a smoother prior outperforming an exact-but-noisy one. We regard this as a plausible but untested interpretation, one that could be adjudicated directly by removing propagation delay from the simulation (testing the first explanation) or by denoising, or adding synthetic noise to, the true connectome before reconstruction (testing the second).

Overall, these results suggest that the Beltrami operator — Wang and colleagues' approach [@wang_geometry_2026] — not only matches but slightly *outperforms* the true connectome, which is a remarkable result given that our simulation is built directly around that true connectome. This is not because the Beltrami surrogate discards structural information wholesale: like the true connectome, it encodes cortical geometry through edge weights that decay with distance, so the two graphs agree on local, short-range structure. What the Beltrami operator lacks is any knowledge of the comparatively small number of specific long-range white-matter shortcuts that let the true connectome connect distant regions directly rather than only through a chain of local hops — and it is precisely this long-range component whose absence, our results suggest, costs little and may even help (see above). This bears on the ongoing debate over whether cortical geometry or structural connectivity better explains functional brain activity [@pang_geometric_2023]. If anything, this comparison should still disadvantage the Beltrami operator, since it is being benchmarked against a ground truth defined by the very connectome whose long-range structure it lacks. Under realistic noise, and in a real rather than simulated brain, it is plausible that the Beltrami operator would perform at least as well, and possibly better still, if fast neural information genuinely travels preferentially across the cortical sheet rather than along white matter tracts — a hypothesis with growing support from work showing that cortical geometry alone constrains a substantial share of observed brain function and dynamics [@pang_geometric_2023]. This is the reasoning behind our decision to retain the Beltrami-based GBF variant (Section 2.4.2) as a full reference method in the clinical studies that follow: if cortical geometry alone can rival, or even edge out, a subject's true white-matter connectome in simulation, it deserves to be tested directly against real, clinically validated ground truth as well.

### Limitations

These simulations let us probe source-reconstruction behavior under fully known ground truth, but they necessarily idealize several aspects of real recordings: known conductivities save for the deliberate forward-model mismatch (Section 2.3.2), a single representative subject, and propagation and noise models that, while physiologically motivated, remain simplified approximations of real cortical dynamics. Some of these modelling assumptions may not hold in real brains, which is precisely why the remainder of this Discussion turns to clinical data, where the same methods are evaluated against ground truths — resection outcome and simultaneous intracranial recordings — that carry their own, different limitations, but are not simulated.

## Epilepsy with Resected Ground Truth

We used this dataset to test source localization against a widely accepted clinical benchmark and to establish a point of comparison with existing approaches. The simulation suggested that connectivity information provides little improvement in single-source localization accuracy relative to CSET specifically (Section 3.1.1), and this dataset, evaluated with an approach similar to the prior literature, largely confirms that picture: peak-to-resection distance did not differ significantly between wCSET and CSET, sLORETA, dSPM, or — included here as a further geometry-based comparator, per Section 3.1.4 — Beltrami, whose median distance came closest to wCSET's of any competitor (Section 3.2.1). wMNE was the one clear exception, significantly less accurate than wCSET, echoing its role as the outlier in the simulation itself (Section 3.1.1). This evaluation has two notable limitations. First, we lack a precise delineation of the epileptogenic zone, only the coarser resected volume as a proxy. Second, localization accuracy here is considerably worse than in the simulation: given the resection volume's typical size, a source localized with the accuracy seen in simulation should fall inside it essentially every time, yet clinical reconstructions instead show a broad, blurred pattern of activity under sLORETA and a more clearly delineated one under wCSET. This discrepancy may reflect an underestimate of physiological noise in our simulations, or the possibility that, by the 50% rising phase, the clinical interictal discharge has already spread considerably.

This observation motivated a complementary metric: because reconstructions at the 50% rising phase already show multiple discrete regions of activity — suggesting either that the spike has spread substantially by that point, or that it never depended on a single region to begin with — we searched for the smallest fraction of the cortex that must be marked active before a cluster first touches the resection. Here the picture sharpened considerably: wCSET required significantly less cortex than every other method, including Beltrami, to reach the resection zone — a large effect against the four connectome-agnostic and CSET comparators, and a more modest but still significant effect against Beltrami, whose reconstructions again came closest to wCSET's. All methods nonetheless reached the resection zone well before chance level, indicating that the true focus is reconstructed correctly by every method but missed by metrics that consider only the single peak vertex; wCSET's advantage lies in how much less of the reconstructed activity outside the peak is superfluous. This is consistent with genuine spread, but also with the now well-established view that epilepsy is fundamentally a network phenomenon rather than a single-generator disease [@spencer_neural_2002; @kramer_epilepsy_2012] — a view under which several regions might jointly sustain a positive-feedback loop that generates the interictal discharge, so that removing any single node of that loop could relieve symptoms even without resecting the point of maximal reconstructed activity. This cluster-based view could in principle help delineate such networks, but doing so is beyond the scope of the present work.

### Epilepsy with intracranial electrode

Intracranial electrodes measure the true electrical activity inside the brain, but they cover only a small fraction of it and record electrical potential rather than dipole current directly. Comparing them to source reconstructions therefore requires an additional, error-prone step: projecting reconstructed sources onto the intracranial channel locations. We adopted Grova's approach for this projection (Section 2.5.2) and defined our own comparison metrics. Grova's original method focuses mainly on the spike peak, considering at most the five time points immediately surrounding it — given their reported 1200 Hz MEG/EEG sampling rate, a window of approximately 3.3 ms. To test whether wCSET improves reconstruction not only at the spike itself but also during its spread, as our simulations predict, we extended this window using the GFP-threshold spike window described in Section 2.2.1: the continuous interval around the peak over which global field power remains above a fixed number of standard deviations of the pre-spike baseline, rather than a fixed five-sample neighborhood. We also excluded Grova's measure of spurious activity, since it presupposes that activity elsewhere in the brain is necessarily an artifact — an assumption at odds with the premise that spike-related activity can genuinely be distributed.

Two of the four subjects have deep sources: despite clear evidence of the spike in the intracranial recording, no corresponding spike is visible on the scalp EEG. Unsurprisingly, no method reconstructs the intracranial channels well in these two subjects, a limitation also reported in Grova's own work. Of the two subjects with a visible EEG spike, the two responded very differently (Section 3.3.1). Subject 1 showed wCSET's clearest advantage: significantly higher spatial correlation with the true intracranial recording than sLORETA, dSPM, wMNE, and CSET, winning a majority of individual timepoints against each; the corresponding temporal-correlation advantage was more modest, reaching significance only against wMNE. Subject 2 showed no comparable advantage: the only significant difference against these four methods was a temporal edge over CSET, with wCSET statistically indistinguishable from sLORETA, dSPM, and wMNE on both metrics. Set against the Beltrami-based GBF variant carried over from Section 3.1.4, however, the picture reversed in both subjects: wCSET's spatial correlation was significantly *lower* than Beltrami's in subject 1, and its temporal correlation was significantly lower than Beltrami's in subject 2 — in both cases a smaller effect than wCSET's own advantages over the connectome-agnostic and CSET comparators, but a reversal nonetheless. Taken together with the surrogate results in Section 3.1.4 and their interpretation above, this is, to our knowledge, the first evidence from real, non-simulated brain activity that a purely geometric account of source reconstruction can match or exceed a connectome-informed one — precisely the kind of test our simulation's own construction, built around one particular true connectome, could never offer on its own. Within each subject, we accounted for the fact that all channels or timepoints being compared originate from the same spike and the same subject by correcting the effective sample size for their autocorrelation, rather than treating each channel or timepoint as an independent observation; this does not, however, address the separate limitation that only four subjects are available in total, which precluded any statistical test across independent subjects. We also did not adopt Grova's own patch-wise reconstruction approach; in exchange, our data offer a genuine advantage over Grova's, in that scalp EEG and intracranial recordings were acquired simultaneously, rather than separately as in Grova's work, where the two modalities could not be recorded together for MEG-specific reasons.

A further limitation of the present framework is its reliance on a cortically constrained source model. Any EEG activity is projected onto the cortical surface even when it may have originated from deeper structures, which is common in epilepsy; the reconstruction can then conserve the correct overall energy while still misplacing it on the cortex, distorting the resulting virtual intracranial signal at deeper channels. Modelling deeper sources would require an orientation-free source model, which would in turn require the connectivity structure to encode each source's preferred orientation — a capability that does not yet exist, to our knowledge. One possible route forward would be to inform voxel orientations directly from tractography and constrain sources accordingly, but we leave this for future work. As it stands, connectivity-informed source reconstruction remains limited to fixed source orientations.

# Conclusion

This work introduced weighted CSET (wCSET), a connectivity-informed source reconstruction method that replaces CSET's L1 sparsity prior in the connectome spectrum with a smooth, exponentially weighted L2 prior, and evaluated it alongside standard, connectivity-agnostic methods, CSET, and a geometry-based Beltrami/GBF variant across three complementary studies designed to probe source reconstruction beyond simple localization.

In simulation, wCSET's localization error at a source's onset differed significantly from every other method, but the practical picture was uneven: a large advantage over wMNE, a moderate advantage over sLORETA, and a small, practically negligible disadvantage relative to CSET and dSPM — differences small enough that, by effect size rather than significance alone, these three methods localize a source's onset about equally well. wCSET's real advantage instead emerged in reconstructing how that activity subsequently spreads: spatial correlation with the ground truth improved substantially as the signal propagated, a gain attributable to the increasing compactness of spreading activity in the connectome-harmonic domain. This advantage proved robust to substantial single-trial noise (wMNE again the one method to break down early and severely) and to considerable connectome degradation, tolerating up to 70–80% random edge permutation before losing its significant edge over the connectome-agnostic sLORETA baseline, and never reversing into a significant deficit even under full permutation. Most strikingly, replacing the true, subject-specific connectome with cruder, dMRI-free surrogates — atlas-derived, purely geometric, or based on the Laplace-Beltrami operator — did not merely preserve wCSET's accuracy but slightly improved it, an effect most pronounced, on spatial correlation, for the Beltrami surrogate. We could not fully explain this surrogate advantage, but propose two candidate mechanisms — a propagation-delay account and a regularization account — for future work to adjudicate directly.

In a large clinical cohort with resection outcome as ground truth, wCSET preserved localization accuracy comparable to established clinical algorithms and to the Beltrami-based GBF variant, with wMNE again the sole outlier, while a cluster-based extent metric showed its reconstructed activity converging on the resected zone with markedly less of the cortex marked active than every comparator, Beltrami included — evidence that the gain in network sensitivity does not come at the cost of focal precision. In a small cohort with simultaneous EEG and intracranial recordings, the picture was more mixed: wCSET reproduced the true intracranial activity pattern more closely than the four standard and CSET comparators in one of the two subjects with a visible scalp spike, but in both subjects it was in turn significantly outperformed by the Beltrami variant — to our knowledge, the first evidence from real, non-simulated brain activity that a purely geometric account of source reconstruction can rival or exceed a connectome-informed one, consistent with what the simulation's own surrogate results had already suggested.

Together, these studies support wCSET as a principled, clinically viable step beyond localization-only source imaging, and more broadly demonstrate the value of evaluating source reconstruction against a source's full, distributed activity pattern rather than its location alone. They also surface a recurring, genuinely open question: across simulation, resection, and intracranial validation alike, a connectome built from actual white-matter tractography rarely outperformed — and repeatedly lost to — a surrogate built from cortical geometry alone. We see three natural directions for future work: adjudicating directly between the propagation-delay and regularization accounts of why geometric surrogates perform so well; extending the model beyond fixed cortical source orientations so that deeper, epilepsy-relevant sources can be represented directly; and validating these findings in larger, independent clinical cohorts with simultaneous intracranial recordings.
